episodes: Ep 158: Hotel minibars charge eleven dollars for a soda whose aluminum and contents cost pennies.
Ep 157: Hoe's 1847 cylinder press printed eight thousand sheets an hour where flatbeds managed only a few hundred.
Ep 156: Sixteen-ounce bottled water costing under twenty cents wholesale sells for four dollars at amusement park stands.
Ep 155: Rail freight fell from fifteen cents to under one cent per ton-mile once iron rails and steam replaced wagon teams.
Ep 154: A bottle of water whose raw materials cost pennies sells for three dollars or more past airport security.
Ep 153: Paper that once cost sixteen shillings per hundredweight fell to three shillings nine pence on the Fourdrinier machine.
Ep 152: Popcorn costing under fifty cents sells for eight dollars inside most movie theaters.
Ep 150: Cordless drill battery packs cost buyers roughly ten times the lithium cells and electronics inside them.
Ep 149: Jose de Navarro's 1889 rotary kiln produced two hundred barrels of cement a day at Coplay.
Ep 148: Polymer sheets worth roughly fifteen dollars become suitcases priced at several hundred.
Ep 144: A bottle of shampoo sells for ten dollars while its surfactants and plastic cost under a dollar.
Ep 143: Alizarin prices fell from fifteen dollars a pound to fifty-five cents after the 1869 synthesis.
Ep 142: A typical bottle of laundry detergent costs roughly ten times the petrochemicals and enzymes inside it.
Ep 140: Blenders sell for fifty dollars while their motor windings hold perhaps five dollars of copper.
Ep 139: Peter Houldcroft's oxygen-assisted laser cut one-millimeter steel where conventional dies once dominated.
Ep 138: Asphalt shingles that sell for roughly thirty dollars a bundle contain only a couple dollars of fiberglass mat, asphalt and granules.
Ep 137: The 1977 Apple II sold for twelve hundred ninety eight dollars when its processor and memory came from standard catalogs.
Ep 136: Vinyl plank flooring reaches eight dollars per square foot against roughly two dollars in raw materials.
Ep 135: Countertops installed at sixty dollars per square foot often contain only about ten dollars of raw material.
Ep 134: Three hundred fifty two dollars bought an RCA television set in nineteen forty-six.
Ep 133: Atwater Kent built nearly one million radios in 1929 using stamped chassis and assembly lines.
Ep 132: Kitchen cabinets that sell for several thousand dollars contain only a few hundred in sheet goods and hardware.
Ep 131: Twenty dollars bought only three minutes from New York to San Francisco before loading coils arrived.
Ep 130: Raw materials inside a typical passenger tire cost perhaps fifteen dollars while the finished tire sells for well over one hundred.
Ep 129: Gustavus Swift shipped dressed beef in ice-cooled cars and eliminated freight on half the animal.
Ep 128: Moving companies bill $90–200 per crew hour while truck fuel and depreciation average roughly $0.90 per mile.
Ep 127: A combine that cost five thousand dollars held only a few hundred dollars of steel and canvas.
Ep 126: A fifty-dollar monthly gym fee dwarfs the few dollars of steel and motors inside each machine.
Ep 125: Parsons cut electricity costs by expanding steam through successive blade rows instead of pistons, dropping the Idiot Index sharply by 1900.
Ep 124: Short-haul air tickets often exceed the jet fuel cost per passenger by a factor of ten or more.
Ep 123: The pneumatic tire cut raw material costs to under two dollars, but early versions sold for over twenty because of manual assembly and patents.
Ep 122: Office chairs that sell for several hundred dollars contain only tens of dollars worth of steel, foam and fabric.
Ep 121: Gillette sold blades stamped from a few cents of steel for five cents each by replacing hand-forged razors with high-volume progressive dies.
Ep 120: Luxury handbags sell for thousands while the leather and hardware inside cost only a small fraction of that price.
Ep 119: McCormick's mechanical reaper sold for one hundred fifty dollars but contained under fifty dollars worth of iron and wood.
Ep 118: Branded plastic toys sell for many times the cost of their resin pellets because licensing and packaging dominate the price.
Ep 117: Quartz watch movements cut timing error from minutes per month to seconds per year while driving parts cost down to a handful of dollars.
Ep 116: Board games sell for fifty dollars while their cardboard and plastic cost only a couple of dollars to make.
Ep 115: Early MRI magnets consumed hundreds of kilowatts until superconducting coils reduced power to just kilowatts.
Ep 114: A hotel room rents for hundreds nightly, yet its concrete, steel, and energy suggest a far lower physical cost.
Ep 113: Laser pits stamped into polycarbonate discs cut album replication to a few cents, far below vinyl's mechanical costs.
Ep 112: Home treadmills retail for thousands while their steel, motors, and belts cost only a few hundred dollars in raw form.
Ep 111: Standardized protocols and volume manufacturing cut pager prices from hundreds of dollars to tens by the 1980s.
Ep 110: Acoustic guitars retail for thousands while tonewood costs hundreds, pointing to markup from assembly traditions.
Ep 109: Excimer lasers cut LASIK's per-eye hardware and energy cost to tens of dollars by replacing diamond blades with micrometer-scale UV ablation.
Ep 108: A mid-range bicycle sells for several hundred dollars while the aluminum tubing and basic components inside it can be bought for under fifty.
Ep 107: When natural rubber supplies collapsed in 1942, new chemical plants turned petroleum into synthetic rubber at roughly one-fifth the wartime price.
Ep 106: A wedding venue can charge tens of thousands for one day when the building, food, and labor together point to a far lower physical floor.
Ep 105: A price check that once required minutes of a clerk’s time now happens for the cost of a few milliwatts of laser light.
Ep 104: A gallon of basic interior latex paint sells for around thirty-five dollars, but the raw materials inside may be worth only a few dollars.
Ep 103: Electric arc furnaces let one engineer melt scrap into specialty steel in hours instead of days by treating electricity and raw scrap as the true starting constraints.
Ep 102: Replacement razor cartridges sell for five dollars when five blades and their plastic housing can be stamped and assembled for under thirty cents.

Ep 101: Cochlear implants once built as single-channel custom assemblies costing tens of thousands now reach a few thousand dollars through multi-electrode arrays and volume-produced ASIC signal processors.
Ep 100: A month's supply of vitamins that costs pennies to make in bulk sells for twelve dollars because the packaging, testing, and shelf fees have never been forced against the raw chemical price.
Ep 99: Open-reel video tape once ran hundreds of dollars per recorded hour, yet a compact cassette using chromium dioxide tape brought the cost down near that of blank film stock.
Ep 98: A running shoe built from roughly eight dollars of foam, nylon, and rubber sells for one hundred thirty dollars, showing how far current methods sit from the material floor.
Ep 97: The Linotype cast full lines of type from molten metal, turning hours of hand-setting a newspaper page into minutes.
Ep 96: Sofas sell for eight hundred to fifteen hundred dollars while the wood, foam, and fabric inside them can be assembled for under two hundred.
Ep 95: Contact lenses once meant grinding individual pieces of glass by hand; now the raw polymer inside each one costs only pennies at scale.
Ep 94: A bottle of table wine that sells for twelve dollars or more contains grapes and glass whose production cost sits well below two dollars.
Ep 93: An ATM withdrawal now costs pennies in power and data instead of minutes of a teller’s time because the process was rebuilt around the physics of moving paper notes and verifying balances.
Ep 92: A twelve-ounce latte sells for five dollars while its beans, milk, and water cost roughly twenty cents.
Ep 91: Silk stockings once cost a week's wages; a fiber pulled from coal and air brought the price to a few dollars.
Ep 90: Ibuprofen that sells for eight dollars contains raw chemicals worth only a few cents, with the spread driven by packaging rules and distribution layers rather than the molecule itself.
Ep 89: Typewriters fell from costly one-off brass machines to something a clerk could afford with a month's pay once production centered on interchangeable parts and cast frames.
Ep 88: A lipstick tube sells for ten dollars yet holds only about fifty cents of wax, pigment, and oils, leaving a wide gap between finished price and raw-material cost.
Ep 87: Vertical shaft kilns once wasted large amounts of fuel on uneven cement clinker until a rotating cylinder made the heat exchange continuous and far more efficient.

Ep 86: Printer cartridges sell for twenty-five dollars while the dye and glycol inside cost pennies to make, showing how authentication chips and refill models keep prices far above the material floor.
Ep 85: What once required minutes of a clerk’s time and a phone call now clears in milliseconds for a fraction of a cent in compute and network resources.
Ep 84: Dry pet food that sells for several dollars a pound begins with commodity grains and rendered proteins that cost only pennies in bulk.

Ep 83: Early matches poisoned workers with white phosphorus and cost more per strike; red phosphorus on the striker plus potassium chlorate heads cut both the health toll and the material expense while opening the way to continuous machinery.
Ep 82: A mattress that retails for fifteen hundred dollars often contains only a few hundred dollars of polyurethane foam, pocket coils, and fabric.

Ep 81: The first commercial hard drive stored five megabytes at a cost that would buy a house, yet the same aluminum platters today hold terabytes for pocket change because engineers kept shrinking the bits instead of accepting the old limits.
First Principles: The Collected Edition, Volume 0
Ep 80: Baby formula is powdered milk, oil, and sugar at a pediatric premium — the atoms are cheap, the can is not.
Ep 79: The first microwave sold for five thousand dollars; the same physics later cooked dinner for under a hundred.
Ep 78: Car insurance costs far more than the crashes it covers — because we still sell the pool through agents.
Ep 77: Polio vaccine fell from dollars a dose to pennies once the virus left monkey kidneys for steel tanks.
Ep 76: Bottled water can sell for a hundred times what the water and the plastic actually cost.
Ep 75: A garment closure once cost hours of handwork. Machines dropped a meter of zipper to a few grams of brass and tape.
Ep 74: A diaper's polymer and pulp cost pennies; the one on the shelf costs several times the materials inside.
Ep 73: Manual laundry once swallowed entire days of scrubbing; electric motors and stamped galvanized tubs cut the machine's price from weeks of wages down to a few days.
Ep 72: College tuition that runs thirty thousand dollars a year rests on instruction whose direct delivery cost sits at a few hundred dollars per student.

Ep 71: The cost of moving one passenger one mile fell from hundreds of dollars in the Wright Flyer days to a few cents by the DC-3, because designers stopped copying wood frames and started from the strength of aluminum sheet.
Ep 70: A generic pill whose active ingredient costs pennies to synthesize can still cost patients hundreds of dollars a month.
Ep 69: Transistors that once cost dollars each now sell for fractions of a cent because engineers reduced them to the price of silicon and a few dopant atoms.
Ep 68: Funerals often total seven to twelve thousand dollars, yet the raw materials in a casket and the physical steps of a service suggest a far lower floor.
Ep 67: Before the barcode, every price at checkout had to be typed by hand; afterward, a laser read an identity printed in ordinary ink for a cost approaching zero.
Ep 66: Textbooks that cost students hundreds of dollars each term could be duplicated at near-zero marginal cost once written, yet the price stays high because of how courses are chosen and paid for.
Ep 65: A pen that once sold for the price of a luxury watch now costs pennies because one company turned micron-level precision into a high-volume manufacturing problem.
Ep 64: A DC fast-charging stall can cost several times the price of the charger hardware alone because trenching, transformers, and interconnection work dominate the total.
Ep 63: Traditional steel plants cost billions to build from ore, yet minimills using scrap and electricity started far cheaper and kept moving up the product ladder.
Ep 62: Sustainable aviation fuel often costs three to five times fossil jet fuel, even though the raw inputs point to a far lower floor.

Ep 61: A high-wheel bicycle that demanded months of wages and athletic nerve became an everyday tool for workers and women once its steel, chain, and tires were redesigned from the loads and materials upward.
Ep 60: Parking that feels free to drivers actually bundles thousands of dollars of land and structure into every rent, grocery bill, and apartment price.
Ep 59: Wheat that once collapsed under heavy grain now yields two to three times more per acre because breeders shortened the stalk instead of adding still more fertilizer.
Ep 58: Elder care costs are driven almost entirely by human hours, leaving little room for the material-cost reductions seen in rockets or steel.
Ep 57: Plate glass once cost many times its raw sand and lime because weeks of grinding and polishing dominated the price — until molten glass was allowed to float itself flat on tin.
Ep 56: Purifying a liter of water to drinkable standards costs pennies in energy and chemicals, yet the pipes that move it often multiply the price by orders of magnitude.
Ep 55: Newcomen engines burned coal to reheat a cylinder they had just cooled every stroke, until Watt isolated the condenser and cut fuel use by roughly three-quarters.
Ep 54: Routine legal documents costing thousands today have an Idiot Index in the thousands because their raw-material cost is essentially zero.
Ep 53: For a century every photograph carried a real cost in silver, chemicals, and paper; silicon sensors collapsed the marginal cost of an image to nearly zero by turning photons into charge.
Ep 52: A prosthetic limb billed at fifty thousand dollars contains roughly fifty dollars of plastic and actuators—the gap lives in custom labor and process, not the materials.
Ep 51: Most food rotted before reaching armies or cities out of season until heat and sealed containers turned harvest abundance into months of usable supply at a small multiple of the raw food cost.
Ep 50: Rail moves a ton a mile with far less energy than trucks, yet the cheaper physics mode still loses on delivered cost.
Ep 49: A catalytic converter’s price is set less by its ceramic and steel than by a few grams of platinum, palladium, and rhodium whose scarcity keeps the floor stubbornly high.
Ep 48: Satellites that reach orbit often cost millions yet contain only thousands of dollars of silicon, aluminum, and electronics — the real expense sits in the process, not the atoms.
Ep 47: Before the integrated circuit, adding each transistor required another hand-soldered wire; afterward, billions could be printed onto a sliver of purified sand for a few cents.
Ep 46: Raising animals for protein wastes most input energy on the animal’s life; microbes could brew the same molecules for far less.

Ep 45: Before the cotton gin, one worker cleaned roughly a pound of fiber per day by hand; the machine that attacked only the seed-separation step raised that output by a factor of fifty almost overnight.

Ep 44: A house built from lumber, gypsum, concrete, and glass still costs many times the value of those raw materials because the expense sits in assembly, regulation, and financing rather than in the stuff itself.
Ep 43: A watch whose price once tracked hundreds of skilled labor hours now costs a few dollars because engineers replaced the entire mechanism with a vibrating quartz crystal and a silicon chip.
Ep 42: A ton of old circuit boards already contains more gold than a ton of virgin ore, yet the cost to recover it still sits many times higher than the metals themselves.
Ep 41: Ice once cut from frozen ponds and hauled across oceans now costs pennies to produce anywhere because engineers asked what it truly takes to pump heat out of a box.
Ep 40: A package can cross an ocean for pennies per kilogram, yet the last few kilometers to a doorstep often multiply the total cost several times over.
Ep 39: Battery packs that once cost several thousand dollars per kilowatt-hour now sit near one hundred dollars because teams priced the metals and assembly energy alone and attacked everything else.
Ep 38: A routine dental filling can cost hundreds while the materials inside are worth only a few dollars, showing where the real price drivers sit.
Ep 37: Intricate patterned cloth once demanded teams of skilled hands per row; punched cards collapsed that labor into the cost of thread and a stack of holes.
Ep 36: Cement that binds our buildings costs many times the limestone and fuel alone, because the century-old kiln process itself is the real expense.
Ep 35: Copper cables costing thousands per kilometer gave way to glass strands worth pennies once engineers treated data movement as a purity problem instead of a wiring problem.

Ep 34: A mile of subway can cost two billion dollars in one city and a tenth that in another, even with similar rock and water tables, because the raw materials and boring hours explain almost none of the difference.
Ep 33: Messages crossed the Atlantic in two weeks by ship until engineers treated the ocean floor itself as the medium and moved a word in minutes.
Ep 32: Burning fuel for heat hits a hard 100% efficiency wall, yet heat pumps routinely deliver three to four times more heat than the electricity they consume by moving heat instead of creating it.
Ep 31: Before interchangeable parts, a musket cost many times its raw iron and wood because every component had to be hand-fitted by skilled craftsmen.
Ep 30: Replacing a lead service line costs thousands of dollars, yet the pipe material itself is worth only tens of dollars — the price is almost entirely in the digging, records, and restoration.
Ep 29: Before Gutenberg a book cost as much as a house; afterward the marginal cost of another page fell toward paper and ink alone.
Ep 28: A century after insulin's patent sold for a dollar, vials still list for hundreds despite raw-material costs in the low single digits.
Ep 27: The real price of artificial light has fallen roughly ten thousandfold since whale-oil lamps, because each generation measured lumens delivered rather than lamps sold.
Ep 26: Most collected recyclables cost more to sort than the raw materials they contain are worth — except for a few that already beat that floor.
Ep 25: Before containers, dock handling often cost more than the sea voyage itself; afterward the entire system converged on the steel-and-fuel floor.
Ep 24: Indoor farms sell lettuce at premium prices, yet the electricity to replace sunlight often exceeds the value of the crop itself.
Ep 23: Two brothers spent a few dollars on fabric and wire to solve aircraft control while rivals spent fortunes on engines that still crashed.
Ep 22: Geothermal could supply steady power anywhere if the cost of reaching hot rock fell to the price of pipe and steel alone.
Ep 21: Before 1909, nitrogen for crops came from finite mines and seabird droppings; the Haber-Bosch process turned the air itself into an unlimited supply.

Ep 20: In 1941 the world’s penicillin could treat only a handful of patients; three years later it covered every Allied casualty on D-Day because the process was rebuilt around oxygen transfer and reactor volume instead of flask surface area.
Ep 19: A commercial kitchen build-out can run half a million dollars, yet the raw steel, compressors, and ductwork inside point to a far lower floor.

Ep 18: The first human genome cost billions and took thirteen years; today the same sequence costs a few hundred dollars in hours because someone treated DNA as millions of parallel reactions instead of one at a time.
Ep 17: Hearing aids that cost thousands per pair contain electronics worth only tens of dollars; the gap is not the silicon but the bundled model that has kept prices high.
Ep 16: An LED bulb that cost fifty dollars in 2010 now sells for a few dollars because its price was driven toward the cost of the semiconductor die and phosphor inside.
Ep 15: Prescription glasses retail for hundreds yet contain just dollars of polycarbonate and metal — why hasn't the cost fallen toward the material floor?
Ep 14: In the 1850s aluminum cost more than gold at the table of Napoleon III because no one could separate it cheaply from its oxide.
Ep 13: Capturing carbon dioxide from air today costs hundreds or thousands of dollars per ton, yet thermodynamics sets an energy floor far below that price.

Ep 12: Rockets once priced at roughly ten thousand dollars per kilogram to orbit now reach a few thousand through reuse — because the question changed from building expendables cheaper to whether the hardware must be thrown away after one flight.
Ep 11: Transmission lines that could cost a few times their copper and steel now run many times that because the real expense sits in permits, queues, and custom builds.
Ep 10: Traditional vaccines grow and inactivate whole pathogens one disease at a time, but mRNA hands the cell the genetic instructions and lets it make the antigen instead.
